Nehushtan
neh-HUSH-tan
proper noun (the derisive name Hezekiah gave the brazen serpent when he destroyed it as an idol)
Hebrew Nechushtan, from nechosheth (H5178), bronze or brass, formed with a diminishing and contemptuous force — something close to “a mere piece of brass.” The name itself was Hezekiah’s own coinage at the moment of destruction, chosen precisely to strip the object of a reverence it had wrongly accumulated.

Biblical Definition

The object Hezekiah named Nehushtan began centuries earlier as an act of God’s own commanded mercy. When fiery serpents afflicted Israel in the wilderness for their sin, the LORD told Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live (Num 21:8). Moses made a serpent of brass, and whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten lived (Num 21:9). Christ Himself later took this exact event as a type of His own crucifixion: as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up (Joh 3:14). But the preserved bronze object outlived its moment. By Hezekiah’s reign, centuries later, Judah had begun burning incense to it as though the relic itself, rather than the LORD who had commanded its making, held saving power. Hezekiah’s reforms removed the high places, brake the images, cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan (2Ki 18:4) — a mere brazen thing, unworthy of the incense the people had given it. A means of grace, kept past its appointed use and venerated for itself, had become an idol; the king who honored the LORD destroyed it for that very reason.

Webster 1828 Definition

The bronze serpent Moses made at God’s command in the wilderness, later worshipped as an idol and destroyed by King Hezekiah, who gave it the contemptuous name Nehushtan.

expand to see more

NEHUSHTAN, n. The derisive name given by King Hezekiah to the bronze serpent of Moses when he destroyed it as an object of idolatrous worship.

The serpent itself was made by Moses at God’s command in the wilderness (Numbers 21).

Whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten by a fiery serpent lived.

Centuries later Judah burned incense to the preserved relic as an idol.

Hezekiah broke it in pieces in his reforms and named it Nehushtan, a mere thing of brass.

Key Scripture

2Ki 18:4 — "He removed the high places, and brake the images, and cut down the groves, and brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made: for unto those days the children of Israel did burn incense to it: and he called it Nehushtan."

Num 21:8 — "And the LORD said unto Moses, Make thee a fiery serpent, and set it upon a pole: and it shall come to pass, that every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live."

Num 21:9 — "And Moses made a serpent of brass, and put it upon a pole, and it came to pass, that if a serpent had bitten any man, when he beheld the serpent of brass, he lived."

Joh 3:14 — "And as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up:"

Modern Corruption

The modern instinct is to assume idolatry always begins with something false; Nehushtan shows it can begin with something God Himself commanded, kept past its purpose and venerated for itself instead of for what it typified.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No one today argues for bowing before bronze serpents, and the word itself is rare even among the doctrinally literate.

The principle to recover is the uncomfortable one Hezekiah’s reform insists on: this was not a foreign idol smuggled in from Canaan but a God-ordained object of His own commanded mercy, and it became an idol anyway, by nothing more than being kept and reverenced past its appointed use. Every means of grace carries this same danger — a sacrament, a hymn, a translation, a preacher, a revival, a church building, even a right doctrine rightly formulated — can be so venerated for itself that it eclipses the LORD it was given to point toward. Hezekiah is commended in Scripture precisely for being willing to break what his own fathers had kept sacred, once it had ceased to serve its purpose and become the object of worship in its own right. The serpent that once meant look and live had become a thing the nation looked at instead of the LORD; Hezekiah’s name for it, a mere piece of brass, is the corrective every generation needs applied to whatever its own Nehushtan has become.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Nechushtan, from nechosheth, bronze or brass (H5178), a contemptuous coinage by Hezekiah stripping the once-venerated relic of its wrongly accumulated reverence.

expand to see more

Hebrew nechosheth (H5178) — bronze, brass, copper; the base noun.

The -an ending gives the word a diminishing, almost mocking force: a mere brazen thing.

Hebrew nachash (H5175) — serpent; the word for the object itself in Numbers 21, distinct from but audibly close to Nehushtan.

The object’s original purpose: whoever looked upon it in faith after being bitten lived (Numbers 21:8-9).

Christ’s own use of the type in John 3:14 fixes its true and lasting meaning, in contrast to Judah’s later idolatrous use of the relic itself.

Usage

"“He brake in pieces the brasen serpent that Moses had made... and he called it Nehushtan” — Hezekiah’s reform."

"“Every one that is bitten, when he looketh upon it, shall live” — its original, God-commanded purpose."

"“As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, even so must the Son of man be lifted up” — Christ’s own use of the type."
